title: The Golden State Dynasty: What Steph Curry and the Warriors Taught Basketball
summary: Four championships in eight years. A revolution in how basketball is played. And a point guard who changed what everyone thought was possible from that position. The Golden State Warriors dynasty deserves its place among the great team sports stories.
content:
Before Stephen Curry, the three-point shot was a weapon used selectively — a tool for specialists, deployed in specific situations, not the foundation of an offensive system. After Stephen Curry, every team in the NBA reassessed everything. The game changed because one player made the impossible look routine.

The Golden State Warriors' dynasty — four NBA titles in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022 — was built on a simple but revolutionary idea: if you can shoot accurately from further away than the opposition can defend, you create space that conventional basketball cannot counter. Curry's range was so extreme that defenders had to meet him at half court. Which created space for everyone else.

The System and the Players

Coach Steve Kerr inherited a talented roster and built a system around movement, sharing, and the relentless search for the best shot rather than the first available shot. The Warriors at their peak were a joy to watch — the ball moved, the players moved, and the whole structure had an elegance that felt more like jazz improvisation than set-play execution.

Klay Thompson, alongside Curry, gave Golden State arguably the greatest shooting backcourt in NBA history. Draymond Green, the defensive anchor and playmaking centre, was the connective tissue — the player whose intelligence and energy made the system function even when the shots were not falling.

What Curry did was not just shoot threes. He redefined the geometry of the game. When you can score from anywhere, the whole court becomes a threat.

The Durant Years

The addition of Kevin Durant in 2016 — joining a team that had just won 73 regular season games — was the most controversial roster move in modern NBA history. Critics called it unsporting. Warriors fans called it genius. The truth was somewhere between: it produced two more championships but also created tensions that eventually broke the team apart.

Durant's departure in 2019, and the injuries that followed to both Thompson and Curry, seemed to signal the dynasty's end. That the Warriors rebuilt — without Durant, with Thompson returning from two devastating injuries — to win a fourth title in 2022 is the most remarkable chapter in their story.

The Legacy

The Warriors' influence on basketball at every level is incalculable. High school and college teams run pace-and-space offences. The number of three-point attempts across the NBA has risen every year since Golden State's first title. Centres who cannot shoot from distance are increasingly redundant.

Curry himself remains the standard by which shooting guards and point guards are measured — not just for his accuracy but for the difficulty of the shots he makes, the range from which he attempts them, and the calm with which he operates when everything depends on the next possession.

The dynasty may be over. The revolution it started is permanent.
author: SportsKeen Editorial
